story_text.value:
In these troubled times it's easy to descent into anxiety and pessimism.

But let's remind ourselves how amazing it is to be alive to witness those historical moments, good and bad.

After the recent acceleration of progress of knowledge all around, it's amazing to enumerate all the things that I, as a kid, though would always remain in the realm of science-fiction, but actually became real: the ubiquity of personal computers to begin with, pervasive worldwide communication network basically for free, conversational AI capable of mathematical prowess, but also the discovery of too many exoplanets to name them all, the launch of hundredth of satellite every week like space is a few bus stops away...

So, what else do you think will go from science-fiction to reality in our life-time?

Just a few suggestions to get you started:

  - discovery of extraterrestrial life forms?
  - fusion based energy for free?
  - routine implantation of cybernetic ad-ons?
  - city trips to the moon?
  - a large scale revolution?
  - terraforming?
  - third world war?
  - bioengineered viruses that decimate humanity?
  - ...by mistake?
  - flying cars ?!? (no, just joking)

title.value: Ask HN: What's the next big sci-fi thing to become real?

story_text.value:
Hey HN, For the past half year I've been working on Slate, my C to Rust transpiler. Slate parses C code as gcc/clang/msvc would, and then translates code to rust. The best supported "flavor" as I call them is clang, with clang flavor I've been able to translate the Linux kernel (built for x86_64 defconfig) and booted the built vmlinux to a busybox shell. Code is here: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-linux. Same for projects like Cpython: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-python, and SQLite: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-sqlite. For an example of a multi-target build, I translated zlib to all targets slate supports with 9 features: https://github.com/takashiidobe/slate-zlib.

Since the entire stack is written in Rust, I compiled to wasm and have a fully client side compiler-explorer esque demo as well: https://slate.takashiidobe.com/.

I wanted slate to be easy to use, and also emit code that a dev would want to maintain. It's one binary (cargo +nightly install slate-c2rust --locked), and comes with a subcommand to set up sysroots (for cross-target builds). Instead of supporting only the clang ecosystem (as many existing transpilers do), I wrote my own C parser stack so I can emulate the three major C compilers for multiple targets, and do things like keep comments, do rewrites based on where functions/macros/definitions come from with header tracking, and also handle flags differently based on compiler. There are currently a couple dozen rewrites, like removing muts, lifting pointers to higher level types, solving gotos, improving inline asm, etc,

Slate aims to support all of modern C, including compiler extensions, like all builtins, intrinsics, inline asm for the three major compilers, and flags. Target support (for now) for x86_64, aarch64, i686, arm32, on linux, windows, mac. Of course this is a gargantuan task but I'm chipping away little by little.

Regressions and testing are a big deal for me trying to scale up the project. I have thousands of tests that run per commit, and do oracle and snapshot testing (with filecheck), so every rust binary translated has to have the same exit code as the oracle (C translated by clang, gcc, msvc w/ wine). That gives me confidence that I'm neither worsening codegen nor breaking any past code as I add new functionality. At this point I have over a million lines of tests, and I'm trying to catch more cases day by day.

Hope you try it out!

Hi HN,

I never wrote a travel blog in 10 years of traveling, so I built one out of the data. Bookings, trips, posts, reviews, check-ins and photos.

- Airbnb, Booking, Agoda and more, parsed from Fastmail

- Every trip from Nomads.com

- Posts from the road, pinned to where I was

- Google Maps reviews, as the recommendations

- Years of Foursquare check-ins and photos

- My Instagram archive

51 countries. 7 years in Asia. $64/night overall, mostly chasing the sun.

Hope you like it! Would love some feedback.

Steve

story_text.value:
I wanted to share evalkit - an open source framework for improving agents that we built.

https://evalkit.inferedge.com/

Like most people, we used phoenix, langfuse, but these are good recording traces, managing datasets etc. But the process around evals, agent improvements, regressions, mapping errors/failures to code or prompts has to be hand rolled. We still use self-hosted phoenix, but mainly as a database.

Our process was trace mining, converting them into evals, getting them reviewed by an expert, and then re-running datasets to create baseline scores or internal benchmarks for our agents.

We found other companies also follow similar processes in-house, but there is no good framework to do everything e2e. So we carved out what we built into evalkit.

- evalkit automatically groups similar traces into one issue bucket (similar to how one issue in sentry can link to multiple events) - Expert review workflow with simple english rubrics (instead of json) - Coding agent first approach - we expect your coding agent to be able to do most steps, and you rarely have to open the UI

An example of how we used it in-house: evalkit identified 89 traces in on bucket, suggested 14 cases, which resulted in 4 merged PRs. We saw 90% reduction in failures, 80% reduction in token consumption (and cost), and 45% in time.

This is pretty early, and we are adding features every few days. If you feel this is useful, or have any suggestions, reach out to us on evalkit@inferedge.com or join our slack community and give us some love by starring us on github :)

story_text.value:
For about the past six months, I feel that American society's views on AI have already fallen into a state of chaos.

People say AI valuations are a bubble, AI can't produce effective productivity, AI companies aren't worth that much money, AI data centers are a waste of resources, and some even think the entire AI industry is just entertaining itself. But then a bunch of people can't live without AI.

Seriously, if Anthropic and OpenAI were willing to sell themselves to China at what everyone calls "bubble valuations," China would be very willing to buy the entire AI bubble.

Then, many people in the US don't want data centers, but they also don't want too many data centers to move outside the US.

There's also another group of people saying Anthropic and OpenAI aren't open enough, believing these companies should open-source their models and shouldn't monopolize AI technology.

Fine, then let's say Anthropic directly releases all the model weights, training methods, training data, and related technologies of Claude Opus 5.5 today. These people wouldn't be happy about that either.

By then, issues like national security, cybersecurity, China's AI development, and technology leaks would probably all come up again.

Besides, how many people can actually run these models? They would still need data centers.

The same goes for GPUs. They don't want others to use them, but they don't want to pay for them themselves either.

They want to pause AI development, but still hope to stay ahead, and hope their enemies won't develop it.

Some people want everything to go back to how it was before, but also hope to make breakthroughs on many problems.

Fine, pause technological development. Then a few months later, even if other "democratic" countries outside China develop it, they'll start talking about things like "industry loss," "national security," "unfair competition," and "how to bring the industry back to the US."

Then they say things about safety and stopping, which all sound very nice, but everyone is accelerating development anyway.

They say valuations are too high, then let them fall. But if they fall to 1/10, they're not happy either.

When the industry is still in their own hands, they complain that it consumes too many resources, develops too fast, and has valuations that are too high.

When the industry really ends up in someone else's hands, they start thinking this industry is extremely important to the country.

You don't want it yourselves, so you give it away, and then cry about it after losing it.

These opinions aren't necessarily coming from the same group of people, but all these internal disagreements are directly reflected in national policies, and directly turn the entire country into a mess.

These policies contradict each other and fight against each other, with absolutely no consensus.

It's like pressing the brake and accelerator as hard as possible at the same time. In the end, the engine will be destroyed, the brakes will break, and the car will overheat and catch fire.

Sometimes I even wonder whether Americans will only have a more consistent view of AI after China's AI proves P = NP first.

And finds a workable algorithm that makes a large number of passwords and cryptographic systems ineffective.

Forget it, I think that's impossible.

But I am genuinely looking forward to next January, when Americans take responsibility for their own choices and really pause all AI construction and development.

title.value: What do Americans want? Their thoughts on AI are so confusing

story_text.value:
Let's assume we want to have a monthly thread for projects that are not vibe-coded or no/low-AI.

Of course this filter cannot be actually enforced, and maybe very few projects are totally without any use of AI (even research could count as AI use). But if devs want to give a honest indication of the level of AI use, what do you think are good criteria for this?

It is an interesting question to ponder. We could have a spectrum of AI use based on the following:

- Is the project based on a one-shot prompt (perhaps followed by subsequent prompts), with no look at the code?

- Are the tests and/or specs human-written and maintained?

- Has AI been used to write any part of the code at all?

- Has the dev actually written any part of the code by hand? What estimated percentage.

- Is pretty much each edit reviewed/approved by the dev, only PRs? Is there any dev review at all?

What do you think is a good criteria to consider a project an AI work, or a human work with AI assistance?

title.value: Ask HN: What's your minimum criteria for a project to be low-AI or not vibecoded

story_text.value:
Hi HN community,

This is Salvador Faria. I've build a platform that allow mid/large organizations to get a view of their digital ecosystem and make informed decisions about their digital properties.

The platform tries to makes things easier for the end users:

- find all company sites

- grades all sites on key categories (end result is a site report)

- "Fix with AI" feature creates fixes for the issues found

Some technical aspects:

- Built with python/django/nextjs/postgres/gcp

- Each page is graded using custom audits and common Google Lighthouse audits

- AI is used to remove false positives (eg: typos)

You can access it from: https://weblidar.com

About me: I've been working in the web development space for some time, and I have built a similar platform for a large company in the past.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I've worked with React Native for years, but I've never been fully satisfied with it. That's why I'm building Hozo, an open-source UI compiler written in Rust.

In short, Hozo is yet another cross-platform UI framework like React Native Web, Tamagui, React Strict DOM, and Lynx.

The idea is to share source code, not necessarily runtime abstractions. For example, a Heading compiles to an h2 on the web and a Text with the header role on iOS and Android.

* Web: Semantic HTML and CSS without react-native-web.

* Mobile: Standard React Native components and precomputed StyleSheets.

* Styling: Tailwind CSS and StyleX with CSS-like text inheritance on React Native.

* A11y: First-class support with platform-specific semantics and compile-time ARIA validation.

* Guardrails: Compile-time diagnostics for both humans and AI agents.

Hozo supports SVG, 2D Canvas, Three.js, and WebView. It works with Vite, Next.js, Astro (including zero-JS static components), Metro/Expo, TanStack Start, Tauri, and Storybook. There's also a component library with an optional shadcn mode, and migration tooling for existing RN projects.

It's still early, though. I'm curious what others think of Hozo.

Docs: https://iray-tno.github.io/hozo/docs/

story_text.value:
Hello folks,

I support AI advancements and have always believed they will create an entirely new class of jobs and dramatically improve productivity.

But if we don't create enough new jobs to replace those lost to AI, how do we prevent deflation? We could be looking at the biggest deflationary period in history.

Just printing more money won't be enough when the deflation is productivity based, will it?

Nobody can predict what lies ahead, especially with disruption happening at such an unprecedented pace.

Where do you see things heading? What new jobs could emerge? Robotics, perhaps?

title.value: Ask HN: Will We Head to Deflation?

story_text.value:
A few years ago talking heads and AM radio personalities went cookoo over AI. The warnings were replete with assertations of total destruction. I blew them off as doomsdayesque viewer/listener headline/listener bastards that saw dollar signs in words.

Assuredly, they completely misunderstood the technology and the intricacies of how AI functions and what it was capable of. They read enough science fiction to regurgitate what sounded like knowledge of the future.

Interestingly, they were largely right in the end. The tech has evolved fantastically quick. The wildest scenarios preposed from previous predicions is becoming realistic.

I do not worry about those scenarios. I do not fear the wildest predictions. Throughout history humans have developed weapons, ideas, technologies, and systems that detractors predicted would kill us all or would lead to insurmountable changes to society.

Electricity is not the devil. The printing press was not a detriment to society.

AI will fundamentally change many things. That is a good thing. Humanity will forever be preserved.

What is Humanity? We will perpetually find out.

Happy Thanksgiving to everyone.

title.value: I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the AI

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Nathan. I wanted to share a project that I've been working on this month.

A few weeks ago, my Rust target folders had grown to about 70 GB across many git worktrees, and I asked Claude to figure out how to stop that from happening. It couldn't find much online, so we started to build our own workaround using some unstable cargo flags. Then someone on r/rust asked why we hadn't just used kache. Someone else mentioned Mr Boxington on a GitHub issue (another great solution).

I also got annoyed that my Claude Code sessions would constantly ask me to reauthenticate my MCP servers, which happens when you run a lot of them in parallel. An agent couldn't find any good "MCP proxy" so we started planning and building our own. I searched Google myself and found MCPProxy.app. It worked pretty well so I wrote a blog post and shared it on X. Some people replied and told me that Executor.sh was an even better solution. They were right, so I switched to Executor.

After all this, I decided to build Talira: A search engine for software that an AI agent can check before it starts building your own solution. You describe the problem in plain words ("my Rust target folders use 80 GB across git worktrees"). Talira searches the catalog using vector embeddings and uses Jev for filtering and reranking.

To try it:

- Search on https://talira.ai

- Add the MCP server to Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user talira https://mcp.talira.ai/mcp

Your agent can also send a report after each search: the problem in general terms, what you tried, what you kept and why. The idea is that it can eventually become a crowd-sourced database of tools that people actually chose and continued using over time.

It's currently in beta and the catalog still has a lot of gaps. I should also mention that I'm aware that ChatGPT and Claude already know a lot and are already very good at search. So there are plenty of cases where you don't need Talira at all. I'll need to collect some more real-world searches before I can benchmark it properly to see if it makes any difference.

I'd like to know if you've ever had any similar experiences. Let me know if an AI wasn't able to find a good solution that already existed.

Thanks for reading!

title.value: Show HN: Talira – Search engine for software, built for AI agents

story_text.value:
I think you've all noticed the "one more thing" with AI, and the many articles to fix it, and that they don't really fix anything at all. If your task ends, so does token spend, so if you ask an LLM to draw a square (metaphor for a moderately complex system), it will forever draw you an approximation of a square, and after stopping it will always tell you that there is still more work to do. Not matter how much you try to force it to finish it just does not. As if physically it can approach but never reach finality.

What has been your experience? Has it improved? How?

title.value: Tell HN: Finality is like the speed of light to LLMs from the labs
